 The Wild's Blueline Depth Is the Product Of A Longstanding Organizational Philosophy
 The Wild's Blueline Depth Is the Product Of A Longstanding Organizational Philosophy 
 Image courtesy of Matt Blewett-Imagn Images
 By 
 Robert Brent 
 - 9 hours ago 
 The Minnesota Wild’s inability to stay healthy has defined their early season. The rash of health issues started with Brock Faber ’s frightening skull fracture. It has continued with Jared Spurgeon , the Foligno brothers, Nico Sturm , and Olli Maatta joining him on the injury report . 
 Minnesota’s depth was a concern entering the season. Therefore, so many injuries this early could be devastating. That hasn’t occurred yet. Minnesota is playing well with a 6-2-1 record that gives them an early lead in the Central Division. One of the main contributors to the Wild’s success has been how easily depth defenders have slotted into the lineup. 
 Players like David Spacek , Daemon Hunt , Matt Kiersted , Olli Maatta, and Zach Bogosian have all played bigger roles than the Wild envisioned at the start of the season. While the team's defensive depth may seem surprising, it’s the result of a longstanding organizational philosophy. 
 Since Bill Guerin took over as GM, the Wild have invested heavily in defenders. From 2020 to 2024, Minnesota spent 43.75% of its draft picks on defensemen, the second-most during that period. Guerin has also signed notable college free agents like Ben Dexheimer and Viking Gustafsson Nyberg . 
 Minnesota has also spent big on the top end of its blueline, signing major extensions with Brock Faber and Jared Spurgeon. The biggest move came last season, when the Wild traded significant assets for Quinn Hughes .  
 Whether it’s spending draft capital or cap space, Minnesota has made it clear it wants a deep pool of blueline talent. That investment has paid off in a defense corps that has weathered several key injuries and remained a strength for a team defined by stout defensive play.  
 With several AHL players and veterans playing roles above expectations, the team still ranks top-ten in the league in several key defensive metrics, including shots against/60 (23.13), Corsi against/60 (52.25) and expected goals against/60 (2.35). Of the Wild’s nine defensemen who have played this season, eight have an on-ice expected goals percentage above 50%. 
 Even more surprising, Minnesota has excelled in areas where it has typically struggled during this era. The Wild are killing penalties at 89.3%, good for fourth-best in the NHL. 
 Jesper Wallstedt 's strong play deserves credit for Minnesota’s goal-suppressing excellence, but the Wild defense has made it easy on their goaltender. In a recent game against the Columbus Blue Jackets, Minnesota limited Columbus to just 14 shots on goal. None of those came from high-danger areas. 
 After the game, John Hynes credited Minnesota’s depth blueliners for sticking to their game and not trying to do too much as a major part of the group’s success. 
 “They’re playing within themselves, and they’re playing their game,” Hynes said . “They’re not trying to do too much. They’re just playing to what their identity is, and that helps when you play a strong team game.” 
 The Wild head coach has also recently spoken about an organizational strategy that has led to so much success for the Wild’s depth defenders. Hynes says that the defensive systems he implements in Minnesota and the systems that the Iowa Wild play under Stu Bickel are nearly identical. 
 “You want to make sure that both teams are playing very similar, if not identical, styles of play,” Hynes said. “The details of the game where you have to be on point when you get here. It’s not like you’re meeting with them about, ‘Hey, we do this versus doing this.’ It’s just more, ‘Play your game. Here’s the routes.’ Everything’s identical.” 
 That organizational throughline lets players transition from Iowa to Minnesota with little change to their responsibilities or the team’s style of play. That approach has allowed players who started the season with Iowa, like Matt Kiersted and David Spacek, to fit into the lineup seamlessly. 
 When the Wild’s injured blueliners return healthy, those same players can return to Iowa without another major adjustment period. 
 The consistency between the NHL and AHL coaching styles is another example of how Minnesota has prioritized investing in its defense. The team spends draft capital, invests significant cap space in defenders, and builds a cohesive defensive structure at all levels of the organization.  
 Those choices allow the Wild, long identified as a defensive team, to withstand injuries without losing its identity. So far this season, that investment has paid off in spades.

 Robert Brent
